title: Simple Interventions: Preventing Symptoms of Depression by Teaching Kids that People Can Change
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart summarizes a study by David Yeager and Adriana Miu in which 600 ninth graders did a single class-period reading and writing exercise on how personality can change. Nine months later, depressive symptoms had risen about 39 percent in the control group but not in the group that learned personality is malleable, even among bullied students. Stuart reads this as evidence that idealistic views of teaching, that it makes a lasting difference, are reasonable. He draws three lessons for teachers: short activities can have long-term effects, freshman-year outcomes are pivotal, and every lesson can affect long-term flourishing. He adds that wisdom matters more than information, and that simplicity and trust beat complexity and control.
points: A single reading and writing activity in one class period reduced the onset of depressive symptoms by nearly 40 percent when measured nine months later.
Stuart argues the freshman year is pivotal because success in ninth-grade coursework strongly predicts eventual graduation.
The intervention worked because researchers identified a problem, applied a theory (the incremental theory of personality) and designed a simple way to deliver it.
He concludes that simplicity and trust, such as trusting fourteen-year-olds to make sense of ideas through reading and writing, can trump elaborate programs.
The piece generalizes from the study to the claim that every interaction with students, spouses, children and friends has great potential, which requires wisdom more than information.
quotes: Okay, stop. Pause. If you are not completely blown away by this, read it again. This, to me, proves the power of teaching.
A single reading and writing activity in a single class period decreased the onset of depression in the freshman year by nearly 40%. And this decrease was measured 9 months later.
While graduation is no guarantee of a great life, not graduating is a strong guarantee of a hard one.
Which means that every one of our lessons has the potential to affect long-term flourishing in a significant way.

What I need much more than information is wisdom. Miu and Yeager weren't swinging in the dark — they identified a problem (onset of depressive symptoms in the freshman year), brought a theory to bear on the problem (the incremental theory of personality), and they designed an absurdly simple intervention for introducing the theory to students.
Simplicity and trust trump complexity and control. Miu and Yeager's intervention was a reading and writing activity — I'm not even sure a teacher was involved.
